title: The Collapse of Antiquity
author: Michael Hudson
desc: Roma destruyó la tradición de cancelación de deudas. Su oligarquía acreedora drenó las provincias como después se drenarían las colonias americanas. La tradición legal romana es el fundamento del feudalismo y el colonialismo.
tesis: Roma destruyó la tradición milenaria de cancelación de deudas que había mantenido el equilibrio social en el Cercano Oriente. Lo que hizo a la oligarquía romana única fue la ausencia de una autoridad superior a los acreedores: el Senado era la clase acreedora. Sin rey que cancelara deudas ni palacio que frenara la acumulación, la dinámica fue irreversible y fatal. La oligarquía drenó las provincias de su riqueza — como después se drenarían las colonias americanas — dejando poblaciones sometidas en pobreza y dependencia. El legado de Roma a Occidente fue sacralizar los derechos de los acreedores por encima de la población deudora: esta tradición legal es el fundamento del feudalismo europeo y el colonialismo.
ideas: Roma destruyó la tradición de cancelación de deudas del Cercano Oriente — el Senado era la clase acreedora y no había autoridad superior.
Sin mecanismo de cancelación, la concentración de tierra fue irreversible — campesinos libres se convirtieron en colonos dependientes.
Roma drenó las provincias como después se drenarían las colonias americanas — el patrón imperial de extracción tiene origen romano.
El legado romano a Occidente: sacralizar los derechos del acreedor sobre el deudor — fundamento del feudalismo y el colonialismo.
contexto: Segundo volumen de la trilogía de Hudson (después de ...and Forgive Them Their Debts y antes de The Destiny of Civilization). Publicado en 2023, aplica su análisis de la deuda como mecanismo de dominación al caso específico de Roma, demostrando que la caída de la República fue consecuencia directa de la concentración oligárquica que la cancelación de deudas habría prevenido.

conexiones.razon: Hudson1 documenta la tradición de cancelación de deudas; Hudson2 explica cómo Roma la destruyó.
Destiny completa la trilogía: de Roma antigua al sistema financiero moderno.
El drenaje de las provincias romanas es el antecedente directo del saqueo colonial que Galeano documenta en América Latina.

deck.label: NotebookLM briefing — The Ledger of Antiquity

quotes.text: Rome's creditor oligarchy stripped the provinces of their wealth much as it stripped Rome itself of public land and self-supporting smallholders. Provincial tribute and tax farming enriched a narrow stratum while leaving the subject populations in deepening poverty and debt dependency. The provinces were not developed but drained.

What made Rome's oligarchy different from that of the Near East was that there was no palace authority, no royal tradition of debt cancellation to restore economic balance. The Senate was itself the creditor class. There was no authority above the creditors to override their demands. That was what made Rome's dynamics irreversible — and ultimately fatal.

Antiquity's legacy to subsequent Western civilization was to sanctify the rights of creditors over those of the indebted population at large. The Western creditor-oriented legal tradition that Rome bequeathed was the foundation on which subsequent European feudalism and colonialism were built.

tl: El interés llega del Levante a Grecia e Italia

the practice was brought to the Aegean along with other commercial innovations from Phoenicia and Syria around 800 BC, when merchants from these regions appear to have begun organizing their trade with Greece and Italy
Tiranos reformistas anulan deudas en ciudades griegas

Mid-7th-mid-6th centuries BC: Popular reformers ("tyrants") come to power in Corinth, Megara, Sicyon and other Greek cities, overthrowing landed aristocracies (often including their own clan members), redistributing land and cancelling debts.

Early 6th century BC: Sparta defers a political crisis over debt and land distribution. Its "Lycurgan laws" abolish silver as money and redistribute the land conquered from Messenia, turning its population into helots to serve Spartan citizens.
Solón proclama la seisachtheia en Atenas

Solon's seisachtheia ("shedding of burdens") is the best attested debt cancellation among early Greek cities. He banned outright debt slavery for Athenian citizens, although not the obligation of debtors to work off their debts as free men owing labor service.
Roma derroca a Tarquinio y nace la oligarquía
509: Rome's last king, Tarquin Superbus, is overthrown. The Republic bases government on oligarchic rule. The resulting class conflict imposes austerity.
Primera secesión de la plebe romana

494: First secession of the Roman plebs, mainly debtors who refused to fight until their subjugation was alleviated. Plebeian tribunes are introduced, but the Senate rigidly maintains intransigent power.
Las Doce Tablas blindan al acreedor

the Twelve Tables that the decimvirs produced were Draconian and pro-creditor, reinforcing the oligarchy's economic power (Livy 3.37). The effect of codifying written statutory law was to make debt foreclosure and other practices uniform, but harsh.

367: Rome's Licinian-Sextian law limits personal land holdings to only 500 iugera (125 hectares). The legislation permits debtors to deduct interest payments from the principal and to pay off the balance in three years instead of all at once.

Livy called the abolition of nexum bondage "a new beginning of freedom." But although debt slavery no longer was legally enforceable under normal circumstances, working off debts in slave-like conditions persisted.
Campania pasa a los contribuyentes de guerra

200: With its treasury bare after paying two installments, Rome has only the public land to turn over, above all the rich Campania. Instead of being settled by war veterans as had been customary, this land is turned over to wealthy war-contributors in lieu of payment of the third installment.
Tiberio Graco asesinado por proponer reforma agraria

they were not able to prevent a large group of senators and their allies from attacking and beating him to death in public with clubs and wooden planks. A reported three hundred of his followers were killed and their bodies thrown into the Tiber.
Aristónico promete una Heliópolis en Pérgamo

Aristonicus, the local claimant, mobilizes the population against Rome, promising to cancel their debts and establish a "City of the Sun" (Heliopolis), a political ideal probably influenced by the Stoic philosopher Blossius. Aristonicus is defeated in 130
Gayo Graco muere defendiendo el Aventino

123-121: Tiberius's brother Gaius Gracchus, continuing their reform program, becomes tribune, but he and his fellow tribune M. Fulvius Flaccus and their supporters are killed in 121 when they occupy the Aventine.

88: The Vespers of Ephesus: As many as 80,000 Romans are killed in Asia Minor in retaliation against Roman tax farming and moneylending. During 88-85, Mithridates of Pontus turns what had begun as a local war in 92 into a region-wide war against Rome.
Sila saquea Asia Menor y se enriquece

86-85: The Roman general Sulla, having marched on Rome to seize power in 88, sacks Asia Minor and imposes a huge tribute, forcing many cities and much of the population into debt to Italian bankers. This helps make Sulla the richest man in Rome by 83.
Revuelta de Catilina por la abolición de deudas
63-62: Catiline's debt revolt. He and some three thousand supporters are killed in battle. A major plank of their program (which Cicero called a "conspiracy") is a cancellation of debts.
Cesar cruza el Rubicón y aprueba la cessio bonorum

49: Caesar marches on Rome and defeats Pompey and his supporters. He allows debtors to deduct interest payments from their principal, and introduces Rome's first bankruptcy law, but it alleviates debt pressures only for the wealthy.
Cesar es asesinado en el Senado

Rome's oligarchic voting system blocked the citizenry from having much effective political force, and the fate of the Gracchi, Marius, Catiline and Caesar had shown Senate power to be strong enough to be immune to democratic reforms to alleviate the debt and land problems. Military bloodshed had settled matters ever since Marius had created an army-for-hire.
Octavio recibe los títulos de augusto y princeps

Rome's oligarchy had been using "kingship" as a term of invective for half a millennium, because "kingship" meant the power to overrule the oligarchy, above all by acting to preserve social order by cancelling debts and redistributing land.

AD 33: A financial crisis results from emperors hoarding coinage in the imperial treasury, aggravated by private hoarding and a drain of bullion to the East (largely to purchase luxuries). Tiberius re-imposes the traditional interest-rate ceiling, and Caesar’s decree that two-thirds of all personal capital be invested in Italian real estate.
Nerón debilita el denario de plata

Rome's trade deficit and fiscal gap forced it to debase its silver coinage, starting in Nero's reign (54-68) when the silver denarius was reduced by about 20 percent. By the 190s about half the silver content of Roman coinage had disappeared

Diocletian issued a Price Edict in 301 collecting many taxes and rents in kind and setting maximum prices for basic commodities that the government needed to buy, but this squeezed producers whose input costs were soaring.
Constantino convierte el cristianismo en religión de Estado

Rome ended the ban on Christianity in 311, and a decade later, in 321, Constantine converted and made Christianity the state religion. The Empire that Christians had spent centuries demonizing suddenly was transformed into their protector
El Concilio de Nicea prohíbe la usura al clero

The Council of Nicaea was convened in 325 under Constantine's sponsorship to help end schisms within the Church. … The Council did, however, maintain the policy of Elvira and Arles forbidding the clergy to practice usury.
Alarico saquea Roma con un ejército de deudores

When in 408 the Romano-Gothic military leader Alaric for the first time besieged the city of Rome [besieging it again in 409 and eventually sacking it in 410], his forces were swollen by many debtors who had left the imperial capital to join his army.
Deposición de Rómulo Augústulo y fin del Imperio Occidental

The aftermath of the Republic saw the distribution of land, money, credit and wealth continue to polarize during the five centuries from Augustus to the deposition of the last nominal emperor, Romulus Augustus, in 476.
Código de Justiniano fija al colonus a la tierra

. The Code of Justinian in 534 spelled out the legal, fiscal and debt obligations imposed on coloni, who were tied to their designated estates to prevent flight from the land. They could not be sold like slaves, but their labor obligations remained attached to the land if it were sold.
